newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Canada makes improved satellite offer at talks.
newsitem.headline: Canada makes improved satellite offer at talks.

text.p: Canada submitted an improved offer in global talks on a world pact to liberalise basic telecoms trade on Friday, providing for the end of the monopoly on satellite services now held by a private company to be brought forward.

A senior Canadian negotiating official told reporters that the offer allowed the end of the monopoly of Telesat company on satellite services to be brought forward from March 1, 2002 to March 1, 2000.

The improved Canadian offer, just a day before Saturday's deadline for a deal at the talks, would also allow the use of any foreign satellite to provide services to Canadians from March 1, 2000, more than two years ahead of schedule, he said.
The official said this had taken Canada's offer to "the last mile" and provided "the icing on the cake" of what he said was a very generous package from his country.

The United States, the world's single biggest telecoms market, has said it is unhappy with Canada's offer allowing 46.7 percent foreign ownership of Canadian telecoms companies and wants the permitted equity level to be pushed above 50 per cent.
A senior Canadian official has said this cannot be changed, arguing that other aspects of his country's proposals made the package a very liberal one.
The Canadian official who declined to be named said Canada believed "the critical mass (in the overall telecoms talks) is here".
"We don't see any reason why a deal cannot be signed tomorrow (Saturday)," he added.

The official said even the Americans had admitted there had been enormous improvement in the nature and quality of offers in the talks over what was on the table when the last effort collapsed in April 1996, when Washington walked away.
He said he could not believe the U.S. would ignore economic and commercial good sense and walk away from a deal now, but agreed that everything was in the hands of Americans.
"I think that at the end of the day, rationality will prevail and we will all sign," he said. "Everybody believes we should sign. As usual, we are waiting to see what the Americans do."
